sections.html:
Middletown, in southern New Castle County, was incorporated in 1861. Its population went from 6,161 in 2000 to 18,871 in 2010 and reached 23,192 in the 2020 Census, helped along by land annexations. Most of the housing around the old center is recent subdivision construction, so a resale house competes with new homes from builders as well as with other resales.

The historic blocks are small by comparison. Anyone who is selling there should expect buyers to compare the house against newer neighbors on size, systems and finishes, and should be ready to explain what has been updated.

Two toll roads bracket the town. DE 1 runs along the east edge with an exit at Odessa for DE 299, and US 301 lies just west and north with exits for DE 299 and DE 71. Inside town, DE 71 follows Broad Street and DE 299 follows Main Street. DART First State buses serve Routes 46, 37 and 302, and there is no passenger rail.

Describe highway access as it is. Buyers who commute north toward Wilmington or south toward Dover will check the drive themselves, and an honest description saves a wasted showing. National retail and food chains have grown along the US 301 corridor.

Middletown runs its own Electric Department and Water/Wastewater Department, and an Amazon fulfillment center and a ChristianaCare emergency department are among the larger local operations. For a seller, the utility side is the part that shows up on the settlement statement.

New accounts for the buyer are set up through the settlement attorneys, so nobody has to visit Town Hall. A late fee of 6 percent applies once a utility bill is seven days past due, so clear your final bills before the closing date.

  • Pay the last electric, water, sewer and trash bills before settlement.
  • Ask your attorney to request a tax and utility payoff figure from the town.
  • Keep your account number and online payment PIN handy for the final bill.

The Appoquinimink School District covers Middletown. It formed when Middletown School District 60 and Odessa School District 61 merged on July 1, 1969. Its high schools include Middletown High School, Appoquinimink High School (opened 2008) and Odessa High School (opened 2020).

Families usually ask about school boundaries first, so find out which school your address feeds before you list and have the answer ready.

The town bills its own property tax from New Castle County's assessed value, while the county and the school district send separate bills. Town bills go out around August 1 and must reach the Town Tax Office by September 30 to avoid penalties. Each month a bill sits overdue adds a 1.5 percent penalty.

Seniors 65 and older who have lived in town for at least a year can apply once for a discount. The application is due before July 1 for that tax year. The discount stays with the residence, so a new owner has to apply again.

New Castle County reassessed every property in 2025, the first countywide reassessment since 1983. Your assessed value may therefore look nothing like what the previous owner paid. Look yours up on the county parcel search before you set price expectations, and call the Tax Office for the current town rate.

Rental owners register with the town, and the unit is inspected at every change of tenant. The first inspection costs $75, one re-inspection is free, and the unit must be vacant and clean. Registration is renewed every three years from approval. Anyone who owns two or more rental units, and any authorized agent, needs a town business license.

Under the town's Clean Hands Ordinance, past-due bills and fees on the property must be paid before an inspection is scheduled. A tenant who wants utility service needs a passed town inspection and a $300 deposit, and only electric and trash can be in the tenant's name. Water and sewer stay with the owner.

  • A mobile home buyer cannot set up service until the previous owner's taxes are paid in full.
  • Tell the town in writing when rental information changes.
  • Ask the town how ownership transfers are handled for registered rentals.

sections.h2: Paperwork to gather before asking for offers
sections.html:
Missing paperwork slows a Delaware closing more than anything about the house itself. If these items are ready, a cash buyer or a listing agent can move quickly.

  • Your deed and the name of the closing attorney you plan to use.
  • The latest town tax bill and the assessed value from the county parcel search.
  • Final readings and balances for electric, water, sewer and trash, all billed by the town.
  • The Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report, filled out honestly, with radon information if you have any.
  • For a rental, the town registration, the last passed inspection and any tenant notices.

If you inherited the house, an exemption for transfers by a fiduciary may apply to the disclosure duty, and your attorney can confirm. A completed disclosure form shows good faith. It is not a warranty and does not replace the buyer's own inspection.

sections.h2: From first offer to closing day
sections.html:
Whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan, the sequence is similar. You agree on terms, a closing attorney opens the title work, and any open tax or utility balance is found and listed for payoff. Then the buyer's side reviews the disclosure report and, if there is a loan, the lender orders an appraisal. On closing day the attorney collects signatures, records the deed and sends your proceeds after paying off whatever is owed.

A cash buyer skips the appraisal and loan approval, which are the steps that most often shift a closing date. Before you agree to a date, make sure your final utility readings and tax payoff can be ready by then. Ask for the agreement in writing, and read who pays which closing cost before you sign.

Delaware's usual realty transfer tax is 4 percent: 2.5 percent for the state and 1.5 percent for the county or municipality. The statute splits it equally between seller and buyer. A first-time homebuyer can reduce the buyer's share by 0.5 percent of up to $400,000, with a ceiling of $2,000.

An attorney must conduct the settlement, and a seller of a one to four unit home must hand over the Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report before an offer. Nonresident individual sellers pay estimated tax of 6.6 percent of the gain, with Form REW EST, when the deed is recorded.

A cash sale lets you choose the closing date, but these steps apply on any route. We buy as-is and do not quote a price before seeing the property.

faqs.q: When are Middletown property taxes due?
faqs.a: The Town of Middletown mails bills around August 1, and they must reach the Tax Office by September 30 to avoid penalties. A 1.5 percent penalty applies for each month a bill is overdue.

faqs.q: Who sets my assessed value in Middletown?
faqs.a: New Castle County sets it, and the town applies its rate to that figure. The county finished a countywide reassessment in 2025, the first since 1983.

faqs.q: Do I need to inspect a Middletown rental before tenants move out or in?
faqs.a: Yes. The town requires an inspection at each change of tenant, with a $75 first inspection fee and one free re-inspection. Past-due bills at the property must be paid before scheduling.

faqs.q: How do utilities transfer when I sell a Middletown house?
faqs.a: Account setup for the buyer goes through the settlement attorneys. As the seller, pay your final bills first, because a 6 percent late charge applies once a bill is seven days past due.

faqs.q: Which school district is Middletown in?
faqs.a: The Appoquinimink School District serves Middletown, with Middletown High School, Appoquinimink High School and Odessa High School among its high schools.
